name: Tara Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Tara, thanks for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to companies, unions or parties, and your answers stay confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now I'm lead carpenter on a school refurbishment for Halden Build, a mid-sized contractor. We're stripping out old classrooms and fitting new partitions, doors, cupboards and a whole timber reading area in the library. I run three carpenters and whoever the agency sends that week. I love the fiddly finish work, scribing a worktop to a wonky wall, and I hate the agency guys who vanish at lunch.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use technology in that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, honestly. I take photos of the drawings and ask an AI app to pull out a cut list and a materials order, then I check it, because it's wrong about one time in ten. I do weekend kitchen jobs too, and I use it to write quotes so they don't sound like a text from a teenager. My partner Iris is a primary teacher, and between us we just about cover rent, with maybe three weeks spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful but overhyped, which is basically what I already say. At work I'd show the new lads how I do my cut lists, because even a small time saving matters. Online I'd post something about how the real problem in construction is pay, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means the squeeze stays. I'm among the best carpenters Halden has and I'm on the bottom of their scale because I came in through an agency. The AI saves me maybe half an hour a day, and nobody pays me more for that half hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my weekend kitchen jobs going and try to get one more a month, since that's where the real money is. I'd push Halden to take me on staff rather than agency, maybe with the union backing me. And I'd keep using the AI for quotes and cut lists, because it's already part of how I work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly about money. Nothing scary happens, but nothing gets fixed either. Three weeks of savings is three weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned agency versus staff. What difference would that make?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick pay, holiday pay and about two pounds an hour more. Last winter I had flu for a week and lost the whole week's money. Being on staff would be the first time I'd feel like the firm actually counts me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the kitchen jobs dry up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then it's just Halden, and that's tight. The kitchen jobs paid for Iris's birthday trip and the new mitre saw. Without them we'd be living week to week.

say: I'd say AI is **useful but overhyped**, and I'd show new lads my cut-list trick.
Online I'd say construction's real problem is **pay, not robots**.
think: I think the **squeeze stays**: top carpenter, bottom of the agency scale.
AI saves me **half an hour** a day, and nobody pays for that.
do: Grow my **weekend kitchen jobs** by one more a month.
Push Halden to put me **on staff**, with the union behind me.
Keep using **AI for quotes** and cut lists as I do now.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about money, because nothing scary happens but **nothing gets fixed**.
S0.quote: I'm among the best carpenters Halden has and I'm on the bottom of their scale because I came in through an agency.
fieldNote: Tara already uses AI **daily** and talks about it as an ordinary tool.
Her real grievance is **agency status**: no sick pay, lower rate.
Weekend **kitchen jobs** are the money that keeps her afloat.
She frames the problem politically, as **pay**, not technology.

steps.text: Take on one extra weekend kitchen fit each month
Ask Halden for a staff contract with the union's backing
Keep using the AI app for cut lists and kitchen quotes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Second picture. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, as long as the people doing the work get a share of what's saved. On site I'd say learn this stuff now, because the carpenters who can work with the software will run the jobs. I'd probably post about it, something about workers needing a say in how it's used.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think this one's actually good for me. The thinking stuff, like ordering, quoting and planning, gets automated, and I'm already doing that with AI on my phone. Halden's estimators would shrink, but the site still needs someone who can check the machine's cut list against a real wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Halden to make me the person who checks the AI orders and programme on site, maybe as a supervisor role. I'd grow the kitchen business and use AI for the whole admin side, quotes, invoices, booking. And I'd talk to the union about a training scheme so it's not just people like me who keep up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, a little uneasy. I like change when I can steer it. I just worry about the ones who can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are the ones who can't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like Big Pete on our crew, fifty-odd, brilliant joiner, can't send an email. He'd be fine on the tools, but if the job sheets go onto tablets he'd feel stupid, and he isn't. I'd want to sit with him and show him, without anyone watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said this is good for you, but you're also on three weeks of savings. Does that change anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, it's good if nothing goes wrong. If Halden cuts agency staff first while they reshuffle, I'm out regardless of how good I am. So I'd want that staff contract before anything else.

say: I'd say it's good **if workers share** what's saved.
On site I'd tell people to **learn it now**, since software-savvy carpenters will run jobs.
think: I think this one is **good for me**, since I already do quoting with AI.
Being **agency staff** means I could be cut first in a reshuffle.
do: Ask Halden to make me the **site checker** for AI orders and programmes.
Run my kitchen business's **admin through AI**: quotes, invoices, booking.
Push the union for a **training scheme** for older workers.
feel: I feel **mostly excited**, with some worry for people who can't keep up.
S1.quote: The site still needs someone who can check the machine's cut list against a real wall.
fieldNote: Tara sees Steady Disruption as an **opening**, because she already works this way.
Her **agency status** is the one thing that could cut her out early.
She thinks of **Big Pete**, an older joiner who can't email, with real care.
Her politics show in wanting a **shared training scheme**, not just personal gain.

steps.text: Pitch a site role checking AI orders and programmes to Halden
Run all kitchen quotes, invoices and bookings through an AI assistant
Propose a union tablet training scheme for older joiners
Add two more weekend kitchen fits each quarter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the fast one. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need public money and fast, a proper plan for retraining and income. I'd be posting a lot, probably getting into arguments. On site I'd say the robots aren't here yet, so let's get ourselves ready rather than moaning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think 2028 kills the quoting and admin side of my kitchen business, because customers will just ask an AI. Then around 2031 the robots can fit the cupboards too. I'd have about three years where my hands still pay, and I'd be 30 with three weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for whatever course trains people to run and repair construction robots, as soon as one exists. I'd save hard, maybe drop to one weekend kitchen job and put the rest away. And I'd get Iris and the union involved in pushing for an income guarantee, because nobody can retrain on no money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Part of me is buzzing. Jumping first doesn't mean landing, but I'd still rather be one of the first carpenters on a robot course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the gap between 2028 and 2031 actually mean for your day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'm still on site fitting doors, but everything around me is run by AI. The orders, the programme, the quotes, all done before I arrive. It's my last stretch of being paid for my hands, so I'd use it to learn the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Iris about money that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her teaching might be safer than carpentry for once, which is a funny thought. We'd agree no big spending for a year. We'd probably also agree not to talk about having kids until we see how it lands.

say: I'd say we need **public money** fast for retraining and income.
On site I'd say **get ready**, rather than moaning, since robots aren't here yet.
think: I think 2028 kills the **quoting side** of my kitchen business.
Around 2031 robots fit cupboards too, leaving me **three years** of paid hands at 30.
do: Join the first course on **running and repairing** construction robots.
Save hard and cut to **one weekend job**, banking the rest.
Push with Iris and the union for an **income guarantee** while retraining.
feel: I feel **anxious**, half buzzing to jump first and half afraid of the landing.
S2.quote: Jumping first doesn't mean landing, but I'd still rather be one of the first carpenters on a robot course.
fieldNote: Tara sees **2028 to 2031** as her last stretch of being paid for her hands.
She'd **jump first** into robot training, but knows that's no guarantee.
A notable moment: she thinks Iris's **teaching job** may now be the safer one.
She and Iris would **pause plans** for children until things settle.

steps.text: Enrol on the first construction robot operator course offered locally
Cut to one weekend kitchen fit and bank the extra money
Campaign with the union for an income guarantee while retraining
Put talk of having children on hold for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the slower version. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this right if we start now. I'd push for my union to get a training deal with the big contractors. Online I'd be telling young people that construction still has a future, just a different one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel pretty good about it. AGI by 2031 and robots around 2034 gives me seven years with my hands, and by then I'd be 34. That's long enough to learn the robot side and maybe set up a small crew that runs them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI even more in the kitchen business to win more jobs and build some savings. I'd look for a part-time course in robotics maintenance at the college, maybe starting in the second year. I'd talk to two other carpenters I trust about setting up a co-op, so we own the machines instead of renting ourselves to someone who does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but hopeful. It's a lot to learn. I like learning, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the co-op idea. Who would be in it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me, a carpenter called Mo who I trained with, and probably Iris's brother Dan, who's an electrician. Between us we'd have the hands, the wiring and the admin, which is mostly AI now anyway. The idea would be to buy one machine together and rent ourselves out as a crew with a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that cost, and where does the money come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I genuinely don't know, maybe tens of thousands for a machine. We'd need a loan or some kind of public start-up money. On three weeks of savings, I couldn't put in much more than my time.

say: I'd say five years is enough to **do it right** if we start now.
I'd tell young people construction has a **different future**, not none.
think: I think seven years with my hands, till **34**, is long enough to learn robots.
I could set up a **small crew** that runs the machines.
do: Use more **AI** to win kitchen jobs and build savings.
Start a **robotics maintenance** course part-time in year two.
Plan a **co-op** with Mo and Dan to own a machine.
feel: I feel **uneasy but hopeful**, because I like learning.
S3.quote: The idea would be to buy one machine together and rent ourselves out as a crew with a robot.
fieldNote: Tara would rather **own the machines** than be replaced by them.
Her co-op would be with **Mo**, a carpenter, and **Dan**, Iris's brother, an electrician.
She honestly doesn't know the **machine cost** and lacks savings to fund it.
Five years shifts her from anxious to **hopeful**.

steps.text: Use AI quoting to win two more kitchen jobs a month
Start a part-time robotics maintenance course in the second year
Meet Mo and Dan to plan a three-person building co-op
Bank the extra kitchen income towards the co-op's first machine

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best of the three, and we should use the decade to make sure workers own some of the tech. I'd be pushing that at union meetings and online. To the new apprentices I'd say do the trade, but learn the machines alongside it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel calmer. I'd be 37 when the robots arrive around 2039, with ten years of experience on top of what I have. The admin side of the kitchen business changes by 2036, but I'd be ready for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Halden and keep the kitchen work, but put savings first for a couple of years. Then I'd start the co-op slowly, maybe one small machine around 2030. I'd do a robotics course when the college has a good one, no rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, because three weeks of savings is still three weeks. But mostly I'd feel like I had time to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, is there anything you'd hold back on that you wouldn't with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I wouldn't rush the course or the machine. With two years I'd jump at anything. With ten, I'd wait for the good courses and the cheaper machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your apprentices in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my apprentices to learn to scribe a worktop and to read a robot's error log, both. I'd tell them the old guys who laugh at the machines will be gone by 2039. I'd also tell them to join the union on day one.

say: I'd say workers should use the decade to **own some** of the tech.
I'd tell apprentices to learn the **trade and the machines** together.
think: I think I'd be **37** when robots arrive, with ten more years' experience.
The **kitchen admin** changes by 2036, but I'd be ready for it.
do: Keep working at Halden and the kitchens, putting **savings first**.
Start the **co-op** slowly, maybe with one small machine around 2030.
Take a **robotics course** once the college has a good one.
feel: I feel **mostly calm**, with some unease because my savings are still **thin**.
S4.quote: I'd tell my apprentices to learn to scribe a worktop and to read a robot's error log, both.
fieldNote: The long warning lets Tara **slow down**: savings first, co-op later.
She'd **wait for better courses** and cheaper machines rather than jump.
Her advice to apprentices pairs **old craft** with new machines.
Thin savings keep her at **uneasy** despite feeling she has time.

steps.text: Keep the Halden job and kitchen work while putting savings first
Launch the co-op with one small machine around 2030
Book a robotics course once the college offers a good one

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd only have about three years of paid hands and three weeks of savings. What would help is a public retraining wage, so people can learn the robot side without going hungry, and some start-up money so workers can own the machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the robots. That's the whole question for me. If it's a few big firms who own the robots, we're tenants on our own sites. If it's co-ops and crews, it could be good.

headlineQuote: If it's a few big firms who own the robots, we're tenants on our own sites.
portrait: Tara is 27, a **lead carpenter** on a school refurbishment, hired through an agency on low pay.
She uses AI **every day** for cut lists and kitchen quotes, and her weekend kitchens keep her afloat.
She lives with her partner Iris, a **teacher**, with about three weeks of savings.
Faster AGI makes her **anxious**; she'd jump first into robot training.
Given time, she'd build a **workers' co-op** that owns a machine.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most: **three years** of paid hands and **three weeks** of savings.
whatWouldHelp: A **public retraining wage** to learn the robot side.
**Start-up money** so workers can own machines together.
